title: Laya - a local model on your own GPU

questions.prompt: A '9B' local model is about 9 billion parameters, stored at roughly 2 bytes each in 16-bit precision. Why does that arithmetic decide which variant you can run on a 4 GB GPU?
options: Because 9B parameters need about 18 GB of file, which does not fit in 4 GB of VRAM, so the smaller flash variant is the realistic choice
Because parameter count sets the price per token
Because a model with more parameters always answers faster
Because 9B parameters cannot be downloaded in one piece
questions.explain: 9 billion parameters at 2 bytes each is about 18 GB, and a 4 GB card cannot hold that - which is exactly why `laya-lab/README.md` says 4 GB VRAM is tight and you should plan for the 9B flash model and expect to be near the limit. The other options are wrong: parameter count does not set a per-token price (the prices in `ClefProvider.PRICES` are vendor prices), a bigger model is generally slower, not faster, and download size is not what decides whether it fits in VRAM.

questions.prompt: Why does laya-lab/README.md recommend setting LAYA_PRELOAD=1 before serving?
options: Because preloading makes the model more accurate
Because the weights are loaded before serving, so the first request is not a slow cold-start outlier
Because the server cannot answer requests until it has preloaded
questions.explain: Without preloading, the first request pays for loading the weights - the README calls it a 40-second outlier. With `LAYA_PRELOAD=1` the weights are already resident when the server starts accepting traffic. In this repo's own report, `run_report()` prints p50, p95 and max latency: one cold-start outlier is invisible at p50, visible at max, and would show up as a p95/max gap. The accuracy option is wrong - preloading changes nothing about the model. The VRAM option is wrong - preloading does not reduce memory use. The last option is wrong - the server starts and loads, then serves.

questions.prompt: laya-lab/README.md says the default way to connect the local model to the harness is to point the existing Jev adapter at http://127.0.0.1:8080, rather than writing an in-process LayaProvider. Why?
options: Because localhost is always faster than the cloud
Because an in-process provider would drag torch into the environment the stdlib-only decisionarena package runs in, and it would skip the real wire format
Because JevProvider already supports a base_url parameter today
Because the local server cannot speak HTTP
questions.explain: Two reasons, both in the README: an in-process `LayaProvider` imports `laya`, which drags torch into the venv that `decisionarena/` runs in - and the repo's rule 1 says the library stays stdlib-only - and it removes the HTTP hop, so the harness would no longer be exercising the real wire format. Note the third option is false today: the README describes adding a `base_url` parameter to `JevProvider` as the plan, but the adapter in `decisionarena/providers.py` still has `URL` as a fixed class attribute, so you would have to add that parameter yourself. The first option is not why - and hosted latency is often comparable. The last option is nonsense: `laya-serve` speaks HTTP.

questions.prompt: The upstream limits table in laya-lab/README.md lists 'Khmer 0.000 at 95.2% confidence'. Why does the README call that the product thesis in one line?
options: Because it proves the local model is useless
Because a decision model that is confidently wrong on an Indic language is a real, purchasable problem - accuracy alone would have hidden it
Because Khmer is too hard for any model
Because 95.2% confidence shows the calibration is fine
questions.explain: It is the clearest possible demonstration of why accuracy is not enough: the model scores 0.000 on Khmer tasks, yet states 95.2% confidence. Accuracy alone would show a bad score; the *combination* of a wrong answer and high confidence is the thing a user can be harmed by, and the thing a better-calibrated model could fix. The first option overreaches - the finding is narrow, not a verdict on the model. The third option is an over-generalisation. The fourth option inverts the meaning: a 95.2% confidence attached to a 0.000 outcome is exactly bad calibration, and the README's own table shows ECE 0.466 improving to 0.081 only after a temperature fit.
